cues.text: A ball made from a sock
Edson Arantes do Nascimento, known as Pelé, was born in 1940 in Brazil.
He grew up in poverty in the town of Bauru.
As a boy, he earned money by serving in tea shops.
His father, Dondinho, was a footballer, and he taught his son to play.
Open our paper street.
The family could not afford a proper ball.
So Pelé usually played with a grapefruit, or with a sock stuffed with newspaper and tied up.
He played for several small teams, and he kept on playing.
You do not need the best things to begin. Make the most of what you have.
Too young?
In Bauru, Pelé also played futsal, a fast game on a small court.
At one tournament, people first thought he was too young to play.
He ended up as the top scorer.
He later said, “That gave me a lot of confidence”.
His youth coach, Waldemar de Brito, believed in him.
In 1956, he took the fifteen-year-old to try out for Santos, a club by the sea.
Ride the paper train to the coast.
Pelé impressed the coach, signed for Santos, and scored in his first game for the first team.
When someone believes in you, it can help you believe in yourself.
Waiting on the bench
In 1958, Pelé went to the World Cup in Sweden.
He was only seventeen, and he arrived with a knee injury.
He had to sit out Brazil’s first two matches.
A team psychologist even told the coach that Pelé was too childish to play.
The coach, Vicente Feola, chose to play him anyway.
Send him on from the paper bench.
Pelé scored in the quarter-final and the semi-final, then twice in the final, as Brazil beat Sweden 5–2.
At the end, he cried as his teammates congratulated him.
When you are hurt, be patient. Your chance can still come.
Hurt again
By the 1962 World Cup in Chile, many people thought Pelé was the best player in the world.
He scored in Brazil’s first match.
But in the next game, against Czechoslovakia, he was hurt while trying a long shot.
He could not play again in that World Cup.
Tap three times to cheer his teammates on.
Brazil kept going and won the final.
Back then, only players in the final got a medal.
Many years later, in 2007, Pelé was given his winner’s medal too.
Even when you cannot play, you are still part of the team.
Knocked down, back up
At the 1966 World Cup in England, Bulgaria’s players fouled Pelé again and again, and he was hurt.
Against Portugal, he was fouled twice more.
Substitutes were not allowed then, so he limped on.
Brazil went out, and Pelé said he would never play at a World Cup again.
But when Brazil asked, he came back.
In the 1970 final in Mexico, he scored with a header, and Brazil beat Italy 4–1.
Head the paper ball in.
He is the only player to win three World Cups.
A setback is not the end of the story. You can come back.
Helping others
People called Pelé O Rei, the King.
The boy who grew up poor became a man who spoke up for poor people.
He supported many children’s charities, and in 2018 he started the Pelé Foundation, to help with poverty and education around the world.
Pelé died in 2022, aged 82, after an illness.
More than 230,000 people came to say goodbye.
On our last page, children play on the street where it all began.
Pass the ball on.
When things go well for you, use it to help others.
